title: Number of Subsequences That Satisfy Given Sum Condition
description: Brute force to optimized: re-scanning the right index for every left index versus a single shared two-pointer sweep across the sorted array, counting with powers of 2.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and an integer target, count the number of non-empty subsequences such that the sum of the minimum and maximum element in that subsequence is less than or equal to target. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

blocks.text: Given nums and target, count how many non-empty subsequences (not necessarily contiguous) have their minimum element plus their maximum element no greater than target, returning the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building Every Valid Team From a Sorted Roster
blocks.text: Picture a sorted list of player skill ratings, and needing to count every possible team (any subset) where the weakest player's rating plus the strongest player's rating stays within a budget. Once the weakest and strongest members of a team are fixed, every other player strictly between them in skill can freely join or sit out.

blocks.caption: Fixing the leftmost and rightmost chosen index lets every index between them vary freely

blocks.text: After sorting, [3,5,6,7]: the valid subsequences are [3], [3,5], [3,6], [3,5,6], giving a count of 4.
After sorting, [3,3,6,8]: 6 subsequences satisfy min plus max at most 10.
Edge case: every pair sums within target
When even the smallest and largest elements combined stay within target, every non-empty subset of the array qualifies, giving 2 to the n minus 1 total subsequences.

Before trying to enumerate subsequences directly, notice that sorting the array first turns "minimum and maximum of a subset" into "the leftmost and rightmost chosen index," which is far easier to count over.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: After sorting, if a subsequence's leftmost chosen index is i and rightmost chosen index is j, every index strictly between i and j can independently be included or excluded, contributing a factor of 2 to the power (j minus i) possible subsequences.

Observation 2: This indexing scheme, by leftmost and rightmost chosen POSITION rather than by value, counts every subsequence exactly once, even when duplicate values are present.

Observation 3: For a fixed left index i, as the right index j decreases, nums[i] + nums[j] only gets smaller, so once a valid j is found, every smaller j (down to i) is also valid, but only the largest valid j is needed since it captures every subsequence for that left index in a single power-of-2 term.

Observation 4: As i increases, the largest valid j can only stay the same or decrease, since nums[i] itself is growing, so the search for the right index never needs to move backward.

This leads to counting by leftmost-chosen-index and largest-valid-rightmost-chosen-index, first re-searching per left index, and then, once the right index is seen to only ever move inward, collapsing that search into a single shared sweep.
Sort the array, then for every left index i, scan the right index j downward from the end until nums[i] plus nums[j] fits within target, and add 2 to the power (j minus i) to the running count.

items: Sort nums so the minimum and maximum of any subset become its leftmost and rightmost chosen index.
Precompute powers of 2 modulo 1,000,000,007 up to n, so 2 to the power (j minus i) is a single array lookup.
For every left index i, scan j downward from n minus 1 until nums[i] plus nums[j] is at most target (or j drops below i, meaning no valid subsequence starts at i).
Add 2 to the power (j minus i) to the running total, then move to the next left index.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: re-scan the right index downward for every left index

codes.python:
def num_subseq(nums, target):
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    nums = sorted(nums)
    n = len(nums)
    pow2 = [1] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        pow2[i] = (pow2[i - 1] * 2) % MOD

    ans = 0
    for i in range(n):
        j = n - 1
        while j >= i and nums[i] + nums[j] > target:            # re-scan downward for every i
            j -= 1
        if j >= i:
            ans = (ans + pow2[j - i]) % MOD
    return ans

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Sorting up front makes "minimum and maximum of a subset" equivalent to "leftmost and rightmost chosen index," which is what the counting formula relies on.
Powers of 2 are precomputed once, so the counting step for each left index is an O(1) lookup rather than a repeated multiplication.
The inner while loop restarts its downward scan from n minus 1 for every single left index, which is the part that makes this version quadratic.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case, since the right index may be rescanned from near the end for every left index.
Space: O(n) for the precomputed powers of 2.
Limitation: the right index search restarts from scratch for every left index, even though it only ever needs to move inward, never back out, as the left index advances.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why restarting the right-index scan is wasteful: as the left index i increases, nums[i] only grows, so the largest valid right index for a later i can never be larger than it was for an earlier i.

What does this monotonic behavior allow: a single shared right pointer that only ever moves inward (decreases), instead of a fresh scan from the end for every left index.

How do the two pointers work together: start left at 0 and right at n minus 1; whenever nums[left] + nums[right] is at most target, every subset of the (right minus left) elements strictly between them is valid, so add 2 to that power and advance left; otherwise, the current right is simply too large for any remaining left, so shrink right.

The core idea: move both a left and a right pointer inward across the sorted array exactly once, sharing all of the scanning work between every left index instead of repeating it.

With the array sorted, walk a left pointer from the start and a right pointer from the end at the same time. Whenever their sum is at most target, count 2 to the power (right minus left) subsequences and advance left; otherwise, shrink right, since that value is too large to pair validly with the current left, or any left after it.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one shared pass, left and right pointers each move inward only once

blocks.text: Each iteration either advances left or shrinks right, so the two pointers together make at most n total moves across the entire array, instead of n separate scans of up to n steps each. Every subsequence is still counted exactly once, by its leftmost and rightmost chosen index, since that indexing never changes, only the way it is searched for becomes a single shared sweep.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the initial sort; the two-pointer sweep itself is O(n).
Space: O(n) for the precomputed powers of 2 (O(1) extra beyond the sort and that array).

blocks.text: The key realization is that after sorting, a subsequence is fully characterized by its leftmost and rightmost chosen index, everything strictly between is free, which turns subset counting into a two-pointer sweep with powers of 2.

items: Forgetting to sort first, without which "minimum and maximum" cannot be read directly off index positions.
Double counting subsequences by trying to count based on value instead of index when duplicates are present.
Advancing both pointers on a valid pair instead of only the left pointer, which would skip valid subsequences that share the same left index with a smaller right index.

blocks.text: Explaining upfront why sorting turns "minimum and maximum of a subset" into "leftmost and rightmost index," and why that avoids double-counting duplicates, shows the counting insight has been fully understood before any pointer code is written.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how do you count subsets without listing them", think: fix the leftmost and rightmost chosen index, and every index between is a free binary choice.
If the interviewer says "how do duplicates affect this", think: count by index position after sorting, not by value, and duplicates are handled automatically.

items: How would the counting formula change if the condition were on the sum of all elements instead of just the minimum and maximum?
Why is sorting by index position, rather than counting distinct values, the detail that avoids double-counting duplicates?
Can you adapt this two-pointer counting technique to count subsequences whose max minus min is within a limit, instead of max plus min?
Two Pointers problems in general, where a monotonic relationship between a sorted array's ends lets one shared inward sweep replace repeated re-scanning.
Combinatorial counting problems that use powers of 2 to represent "every subset of a fixed group of free elements."

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time in the worst case; the optimized two-pointer sweep runs in O(n log n) time, dominated entirely by the initial sort. Both use O(n) space for the precomputed powers of 2.

items: Pattern: sort, then count subsequences by their leftmost and rightmost chosen index using a two-pointer sweep and powers of 2.
Core Idea: after sorting, every subsequence is uniquely identified by its leftmost and rightmost chosen index, and every index strictly between contributes a free factor of 2.
Time: O(n squared) worst case for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized two-pointer sweep.
Space: O(n) for the precomputed powers of 2 in both versions.
Most Important Observation: as the left index advances, the largest valid right index only ever moves inward, letting one shared sweep replace a fresh scan per left index.
Interview Difficulty: the two-pointer mechanics are simple once sorted; recognizing the leftmost/rightmost-index counting trick is the real insight.
One line memory trick: sort, then count by leftmost and rightmost chosen position, powers of 2 for everything in between.
